name: Reading Comprehension
description: Authentic reading passages of 100 to 200 words on education, technology, travel, hobbies, health, environment, work, communication, science and culture, with main idea, detail, inference and vocabulary questions.

passages.title: A Library on Wheels
passages.content:
When Maria Kovalenko retired from teaching, her friends expected her to spend more time in her garden. Instead, she bought an old minibus, took out the seats and fitted it with shelves.

For the first month the bus stood outside her house while she painted it and sorted the books that neighbours had given her. Some of them were in poor condition, and she spent her evenings repairing covers with tape and glue. By the spring she had nearly nine hundred books, and she began to drive to three villages that no longer had a library of their own.

At first the visits were quiet. A few pensioners came to borrow detective stories, and children looked through the windows but did not come in. Maria soon realised that the children were not afraid of books; they were afraid of breaking something that looked so carefully arranged. So she put a box of old comics by the door with a sign that said 'Take one, bring one'. Within a week the box was empty, and the children were asking what else she had.

The bus now visits seven villages every fortnight. Maria no longer drives it alone: two of her former pupils share the driving, and a local shop pays for the fuel in exchange for a small advertisement on the side. Readers can order books by phone, and Maria writes their requests in a notebook that she keeps on the dashboard.

Asked why she did it, Maria says that she was never trying to save reading. 'People did not stop reading,' she explains. 'They stopped having a place to find the next book. The bus is just a way of bringing that place a little closer.'

passages.title: The Boy Who Fixed the Village Clock
passages.content:
For as long as anyone could remember, the clock on the old school building in Hartley had shown twenty past four. Visitors found it charming, (1) ______. So when fifteen-year-old Tom Price climbed a ladder with a toolbox one Saturday morning, most people assumed he would soon give up.

Tom had become interested in clocks after finding a broken alarm clock in his grandfather's shed. He took it apart, (2) ______, and put it back together until it worked. After that he read everything he could find about old mechanisms and watched hours of videos (3) ______.

The school clock was a far bigger challenge. Several parts had rusted, and one gear was missing completely. Tom made a careful drawing of it and asked a local engineering company (4) ______. The company agreed and even refused to take any money for the work.

It took him almost three months of weekends. On the day the clock finally started, a small crowd gathered in the square, and the head teacher (5) ______.

Tom now has a waiting list of neighbours with broken clocks. He says he enjoys the work because every mechanism is a puzzle, (6) ______.

passages.title: The Girl Who Mapped Her Town's Trees
passages.content:
When fourteen-year-old Solomiia Bondar noticed that several old chestnut trees on her street had been cut down, she wanted to know how many trees her town actually had. Nobody could tell her. The council kept records only of the trees in the central park, and even those were ten years out of date.

So Solomiia decided to count them herself. Every weekend for a whole summer she walked round a different district with a notebook, a tape measure and her phone. For each tree she recorded the species, measured the trunk and took a photo, then marked it on a free online map. At first her friends joked that she was spending her holidays talking to trees. By August, however, three of them had joined her, and a local teacher had shown them how to recognise diseased branches.

The map grew to more than four thousand trees. It showed something nobody had expected: the newer districts had almost no trees at all, while the old centre had lost a quarter of its chestnuts in ten years. When Solomiia presented the map at a council meeting, the adults in the room were silent for a moment. Then the head of the environment department asked whether they could use it.

Today the map is updated by volunteers from four schools, and the council checks it before approving any building work. Last spring the town planted six hundred young trees, most of them in the districts the map had shown to be bare. Solomiia, now at university, still gets messages from people who have spotted a tree that is not on the map. 'I did not set out to change anything,' she says. 'I just wanted an answer to a simple question.'

passages.title: The Orchestra from the Landfill
passages.content:
Cateura, a community on the edge of Paraguay's capital, Asunción, lies next to a huge landfill site. Many families there make a living by collecting and selling things that other people have thrown away. In the mid-2000s, an environmental worker called Favio Chávez came to the area to help with a recycling project. He was also a musician, and he began teaching music to a few local children.

There was a problem. A new violin cost more than many families earned in months, and there were never enough instruments to go round. So Chávez asked Nicolás Gómez, a local rubbish collector with a talent for building things, whether he could make instruments out of what the landfill offered. Gómez turned an old oil drum into a cello and made violins from tins and wooden boxes, using old forks and spoons for some of the parts.

The sound surprised everyone, including the children. The group became known as the Recycled Orchestra, and a film about them carried their story around the world. Since then the orchestra has performed in many countries and has shared the stage with well-known musicians.

For the young players, however, the most important change was not the travel. Several of them have gone on to study music, and some now teach younger children in Cateura. As Chávez once put it, the world sends them rubbish, and they send back music.

passages.title: The Stranger on the Night Train
passages.content:
Olha had taken the night train from Lviv to Kharkiv many times, but she had never shared her compartment with anyone (1) ______. The man in the seat opposite was about seventy and was studying a map so old that its edges had turned brown.

When the train stopped in the middle of a field for over an hour, he folded the map (2) ______. He told her that he had been born in a village near the railway line, a village that no longer existed. As a boy, he had watched the trains pass (3) ______.

Olha asked him why he had never come back before. He explained that he had spent most of his life abroad (4) ______. Now, after the death of his wife, he had finally decided to find the place where his house had stood.

At dawn the train slowed down near a row of old poplars. The man pressed his face to the window (5) ______. 'There,' he whispered, pointing at an empty field. Olha saw nothing but grass, (6) ______.

questions.title:
Read the text and answer the question.

The school library at Brookfield was almost closed three years ago. Fewer than twenty pupils used it each week, and the governors argued that the space would be better used as an extra classroom. Instead, a new librarian persuaded them to give her one term to change things. She moved the shelves away from the walls to create small reading corners, ordered graphic novels alongside the classics, and opened the room at lunchtime for a book club that pupils themselves ran. Borrowing rose slowly at first, then sharply. By the end of the year, more than two hundred pupils were using the library every week, and teachers reported that reluctant readers were finishing whole books for the first time. The governors quietly abandoned the plan to convert the room. What had seemed to be a problem of space, the librarian later said, had really been a problem of welcome.

What was the governors' original plan for the library?
options: To turn the room into an extra classroom.
To move the library to a larger building.
To replace the librarian with a volunteer.
To open the room only at lunchtime.
questions.explanation: У тексті прямо сказано, що рада збиралася перетворити приміщення на додатковий клас.

questions.title:
Read the text and answer the question.

Before digital maps, most drivers kept a folded paper atlas in the car and planned a route the night before a long journey. Today a phone recalculates the route every few seconds, warns of delays and suggests a different road before the driver has even noticed the queue. The gain in convenience is obvious. What is less obvious is the cost. Studies of people who rely heavily on turn-by-turn navigation suggest that they form weaker mental maps of the places they drive through. They arrive without much idea of how the streets connect, and they struggle more than other drivers when the signal is lost. Researchers are careful not to call this harm. The brain, they point out, has always handed routine work to tools, from written lists to calculators. The question is simply which skills we are content to give away, and which ones we would rather keep.

What did drivers typically do before digital maps?
options: They planned the route in advance using a paper atlas.
They asked for directions at every junction.
They avoided long journeys altogether.
They memorised the whole road network.
questions.explanation: До цифрових карт водії планували маршрут заздалегідь за паперовим атласом.

questions.title:
Read the text and answer the question.

Night trains were once dismissed as a relic. Airlines were faster and often cheaper, and through the 1990s one European operator after another withdrew its sleeper services. In the last few years, however, several routes have quietly reopened. Part of the reason is environmental: a sleeper produces a small fraction of the emissions of a short flight. Part of it is practical. A passenger who boards at ten in the evening and steps onto a city-centre platform at seven the next morning has travelled and slept at the same time, and has paid nothing for a hotel room. The carriages themselves have changed less than the timetables. Compartments are still narrow and the corridors still rattle. Regular travellers insist that this is part of the appeal, and that arriving slowly is a different experience from arriving quickly.

Why did European operators withdraw sleeper services in the 1990s?
options: Flying was faster and frequently cheaper.
The carriages had become unsafe.
Passengers complained about the noise.
Governments banned overnight travel.
questions.explanation: Нічні поїзди скасовували, бо літак був швидшим і часто дешевшим.

questions.title:
Read the text and answer the question.

Bread making looks simple until you try it. Flour, water, salt and yeast are the whole list of ingredients, and yet two bakers working side by side from the same recipe can produce very different loaves. The reason is that almost everything depends on conditions the recipe cannot control: the temperature of the kitchen, the age of the yeast, how vigorously the dough is worked and how patiently it is left alone. Beginners usually make the same mistake, which is to hurry. Dough that has not risen long enough produces a heavy loaf with a tight crumb, and no amount of extra baking will repair it. Experienced bakers talk less about technique than about reading the dough, by which they mean noticing when it is ready rather than looking at the clock. That habit of attention, many of them say, is the real skill.

Why can two bakers using the same recipe get different results?
options: Conditions such as temperature and timing are not in the recipe.
Recipes are usually written incorrectly.
Flour varies enormously between shops.
Ovens are never the same temperature.
questions.explanation: Рецепт не описує умов — температури й часу, тому результат різний.

questions.title:
Read the text and answer the question.

For most of the twentieth century, sleep was treated as an empty space between periods of useful activity, and shortening it was widely admired. Research over the past three decades has reversed that view completely. During sleep the brain does not switch off; it consolidates what was learnt during the day, clears waste products that accumulate in waking hours and regulates the hormones that govern appetite and stress. People who regularly sleep fewer than six hours perform measurably worse on tasks requiring sustained attention, and, more worryingly, they tend to underestimate how impaired they are. This last finding troubles researchers most. A tired driver who knows they are tired can stop; one who feels alert while functioning poorly is far harder to protect. Public health campaigns have therefore begun to focus less on the number of hours and more on helping people recognise the signs they are missing.

How was sleep generally regarded for most of the twentieth century?
options: As unproductive time that it was admirable to cut short.
As a medical condition requiring treatment.
As the most important part of the day.
As a habit that varied with the seasons.
questions.explanation: Більшу частину XX століття сон вважали непродуктивним часом, який похвально скорочувати.

questions.title:
Read the text and answer the question.

City councils across Europe have begun planting trees at a rate not seen for a generation, and the reasoning has shifted. Trees were once planted chiefly because they were pleasant to look at. They are now planted as infrastructure. A mature street tree cools the air around it by several degrees on a hot day, intercepts rainfall that would otherwise overwhelm the drains, and traps a measurable quantity of the fine particles produced by traffic. None of these benefits arrives quickly. A sapling delivers almost nothing in its first decade, which is precisely why planting programmes are vulnerable: the councillors who pay for them will not be in office when the trees begin to work. Cities that have succeeded tend to be those that made maintenance, rather than planting, the measure of success. Counting the trees still alive after ten years turns out to be a far more demanding target than counting the ones put into the ground.

How has the reason for planting street trees changed?
options: Trees are now valued as infrastructure rather than decoration.
Trees are now planted only in wealthy districts.
Councils now plant trees to replace drains.
Trees are chosen for their appearance in winter.
questions.explanation: Дерева тепер розглядають як інфраструктуру, а не як оздоблення.

questions.title:
Read the text and answer the question.

City councils across Europe have begun planting trees at a rate not seen for a generation, and the reasoning has shifted. Trees were once planted chiefly because they were pleasant to look at. They are now planted as infrastructure. A mature street tree cools the air around it by several degrees on a hot day, intercepts rainfall that would otherwise overwhelm the drains, and traps a measurable quantity of the fine particles produced by traffic. None of these benefits arrives quickly. A sapling delivers almost nothing in its first decade, which is precisely why planting programmes are vulnerable: the councillors who pay for them will not be in office when the trees begin to work. Cities that have succeeded tend to be those that made maintenance, rather than planting, the measure of success. Counting the trees still alive after ten years turns out to be a far more demanding target than counting the ones put into the ground.

Which benefit of a mature street tree is mentioned?
options: It intercepts rain that would otherwise flood the drains.
It reduces noise from passing traffic.
It provides fruit for local residents.
It prevents the road surface from cracking.
questions.explanation: Згадано, що доросле дерево перехоплює дощ, який інакше перевантажив би стоки.

questions.title:
Read the text and answer the question.

When large numbers of employees began working from home, the debate was framed as a simple choice between the office and the kitchen table. Several years on, that framing looks too crude. Surveys consistently find that people working remotely report fewer interruptions and better concentration on individual tasks, while managers report that the work which suffers is the kind nobody schedules: the overheard question, the quick correction, the informal training that new staff absorb by sitting near experienced colleagues. Neither side of this disagreement is wrong, because they are describing different kinds of work. Organisations that have adapted well have generally stopped asking where people should sit and started asking what each activity actually requires. Deep individual work is protected at home; collaboration and training are deliberately concentrated into the days when everyone is present.

Why does the writer say the original framing of the debate was too crude?
options: The choice is not simply between two places to sit.
Very few people actually worked from home.
The surveys were carried out incorrectly.
Managers were not consulted at the time.
questions.explanation: Автор каже, що вибір не зводиться до двох місць, де сидіти.

questions.title:
Read the text and answer the question.

Learners often assume that the hardest part of a foreign language is grammar, and are surprised to discover how much trouble they have with small talk. The grammar of a conversation about the weather is trivial; the difficulty lies elsewhere. Knowing how long an answer should be, when a question is genuine and when it is merely a greeting, how much enthusiasm is expected and when it is acceptable to say nothing at all are all conventions that vary sharply between cultures and are almost never taught. A learner with excellent grammar who answers a casual question at length may be understood perfectly and still seem odd. This is why many teachers now build short, apparently trivial exchanges into lessons. The aim is not to practise vocabulary but to give learners a feel for the shape of ordinary talk.

What do learners commonly find surprising?
options: That small talk causes more difficulty than grammar.
That grammar is rarely taught in modern courses.
That native speakers avoid discussing the weather.
That vocabulary is learnt faster than they expect.
questions.explanation: Учнів дивує, що світська розмова дається важче за граматику.

questions.title:
Read the text and answer the question.

Ice cores drilled from the Antarctic ice sheet are among the most informative objects in climate science, and their value depends on a simple physical accident. As snow accumulates and is compressed into ice, it traps tiny bubbles of the air that surrounded it. Those bubbles are not a proxy or an estimate; they are samples of the actual atmosphere of the year in which the snow fell. A core several kilometres long therefore contains a sequential archive stretching back hundreds of thousands of years, from which the composition of past atmospheres can be measured directly. The chief difficulty is not extraction but dating. Layers near the surface are distinct and can be counted like tree rings, but under the pressure of the ice above them the deeper layers thin and deform until individual years become indistinguishable, and researchers must turn to indirect methods whose margins of error widen with depth.

What makes the bubbles in an ice core so valuable?
options: They are actual samples of the atmosphere of the year the snow fell.
They indicate how much snow fell in a given year.
They reveal the temperature at the surface of the ice.
They contain traces of ancient plant material.
questions.explanation: Бульбашки цінні тим, що це справжні зразки атмосфери того року, коли випав сніг.

questions.title:
Read the text and answer the question.

Few debates in the museum world are as difficult as the question of restitution. Many of the objects in European collections arrived during periods of colonial rule, under conditions that would not be accepted today, and the countries they came from have asked for them back. The arguments against returning them have grown weaker over time. Claims that receiving institutions lack the facilities to care for objects have been answered by the construction of well-equipped museums in the countries concerned, and the fear that one return would empty every gallery in Europe has not been borne out where returns have taken place. What remains genuinely hard is the detail. Ownership records are often incomplete, several parties may have a legitimate claim to the same object, and legislation in some countries actively prevents national collections from giving anything away. Progress, where it has been made, has usually come from long negotiation rather than from any single decision of principle.

What has weakened the argument about receiving institutions?
options: Well-equipped museums have been built in the countries making claims.
Fewer objects are now requested than in the past.
European museums have run out of storage space.
International law now requires immediate return.
questions.explanation: Аргумент про приймаючі установи ослаб, бо в країнах-заявниках побудували добре обладнані музеї.

questions.explanation: Кожен фрагмент має пасувати і граматично, і за змістом: після коми в (1) потрібне протиставлення (but), у (4) — непряме питання після asked (whether…), у (6) — продовження думки про головоломки. Фрагмент про дідуся-вчителя й обіцянку ради не пов’язані ні з одним пропуском.

questions.title: Why did Solomiia start counting the trees?
options: She could not find out how many there were.
Her teacher gave her a summer project.
The council asked schools for help.
She wanted to protect the central park.
questions.explanation: У першому абзаці: вона хотіла знати, скільки в місті дерев, але ніхто не міг їй сказати.

questions.title: What was wrong with the council's records?
options: They were old and covered only one park.
They had been lost during a flood.
They counted only chestnut trees.
They were kept secret from the public.
questions.explanation: Рада мала записи лише про центральний парк, і ті застаріли на десять років.

questions.title: How did her friends react at first?
options: They made fun of her.
They refused to speak to her.
They offered to pay for the map.
They told her parents about it.
questions.explanation: Спершу друзі жартували, що вона проводить канікули, розмовляючи з деревами, — тобто глузували.

questions.title: What did the map reveal?
options: New districts had very few trees.
Most trees in the centre were diseased.
The park had more trees than recorded.
Volunteers had counted some trees twice.
questions.explanation: Мапа показала, що в нових районах майже немає дерев, а старий центр утратив чверть каштанів.

questions.title: What does Solomiia say about her project?
options: It began as simple curiosity.
She planned it to change city policy.
She did it to get into university.
It was harder than she had expected.
questions.explanation: Її слова в кінці: вона не збиралася нічого змінювати, а просто хотіла відповіді на просте запитання.

questions.title: How do many families in Cateura earn money?
options: By selling things found in waste.
By working at a music school.
By building houses near the capital.
By making instruments for tourists.
questions.explanation: У першому абзаці: багато родин живуть з того, що збирають і продають викинуті речі.

questions.title: Why did Chávez ask Nicolás Gómez for help?
options: Real instruments were too expensive to buy.
Gómez had played in a famous orchestra.
The children refused to learn without him.
Gómez owned the land next to the site.
questions.explanation: Скрипка коштувала більше, ніж родина заробляла за місяці, а інструментів бракувало — тому їх вирішили робити з відходів.

questions.title: What was the cello made from?
options: an oil drum
a wooden box
old tins
a set of forks
questions.explanation: Gómez turned an old oil drum into a cello — віолончель зробили з бочки з-під мастила.

questions.title: What made the orchestra known around the world?
options: a film about the group
a radio competition
a concert in Asunción
a famous violin teacher
questions.explanation: У третьому абзаці: історію оркестру рознесла світом стрічка про нього.

questions.title: According to the text, what mattered most for the young musicians?
options: the chance of a future in music
the opportunity to travel abroad
meeting famous musicians on stage
earning money from their concerts
questions.explanation: Текст прямо каже, що найважливішою зміною були не подорожі: дехто вступив учитися музики, дехто вже навчає менших.

questions.title: Read the descriptions of summer camps (1–6). Match each camp to what it offers (A–H). There are two choices you do not need to use.
pairs: Forest Trail Camp. Campers spend two weeks in tents deep in the Carpathian forest. Every day starts with a hike, and by the end of the camp everyone can read a map, light a fire safely and find their way with a compass.
teaches you to cope in the wild
Code and Create. In this city camp, teenagers design their own video game from scratch. Mornings are for coding lessons, and afternoons are for drawing characters and testing each other's games.
lets you build something digital
Riverside Arts. Held in an old mill by the river, this camp is for young painters and sculptors. It ends with a weekend exhibition that is open to everyone in the town.
shows participants' work to visitors
Speak Up! Every activity at this two-week camp, from cooking to football, happens in English. Groups are small, and each evening students record a short podcast about their day.
improves a language through daily activities
Blue Wave Sailing. Young sailors learn to handle small boats on a large lake. No experience is needed, but everyone must be able to swim fifty metres before the course begins.
asks for a skill before you can join
Star Gazers. Far from city lights, this camp mixes science and adventure. Participants build a simple telescope and spend clear nights watching the planets with an astronomer.
involves staying up late
extraChoices: is only for children under ten
offers free transport from the city
questions.explanation: Табір у лісі вчить виживати на природі; Code and Create — створювати гру; Riverside Arts завершується виставкою для містян; у Speak Up! усе відбувається англійською; для вітрильного курсу треба заздалегідь уміти плавати; Star Gazers спостерігає за планетами вночі. Про дітей до десяти років і безкоштовний трансфер не йдеться ніде.

questions.title: Read the notices (1–5). Match each notice to what it is about (A–H). There are three choices you do not need to use.
pairs: The swimming pool will be closed from 3 to 10 July while the changing rooms are repaired. All season tickets will be extended by one week.
a place that will not be open for a while
Found in Room 12 after Tuesday's lesson: a black umbrella and a blue scarf. Please ask at the reception desk before Friday.
things that someone left behind
Volunteers wanted! Help us plant trees in Central Park on Saturday morning. Gloves and tools are provided; just bring some water.
a request for help
From Monday, the number 42 bus will stop at the new bridge instead of Market Street. The timetables at every stop have been updated.
a change to a route
Our café now offers students 20% off every weekday between 2 and 5 pm. Just show your student card at the till.
a lower price for some customers
questions.explanation: Басейн тимчасово зачинено; у кабінеті 12 знайшли забуті речі; волонтерів кличуть садити дерева; автобус 42 змінює маршрут; кафе дає студентам знижку. Вакансії, конкурсу чи загубленої тварини в оголошеннях немає.

questions.title: Read the text 'The Stranger on the Night Train'. Choose from the fragments (A–H) the one which best fits each gap (1–6). There are two fragments you do not need to use.
pairs: quite as interesting as this
and started to talk
and dreamt of where they were going
and had always been too busy to return
as if he were a child again
yet she nodded as though she could see it too
extraChoices: because the tickets had been sold out
while his wife slept in the next carriage
questions.explanation: Після anyone у (1) потрібне порівняння з цим попутником; після folded the map у (2) — наступна дія; у (3) продовжується спогад про потяги; у (4) — пояснення, чому він не повертався; у (5) — як він дивився у вікно; у (6) yet протиставляє порожнє поле кивку Ольги. Фрагмент про розпродані квитки не пасує ні до чого, а про дружину в сусідньому вагоні суперечить тексту: дружина померла.
